Préface p16.text: In the idea of men of modern times, however, the grotesque plays an enormous part. It is found everywhere; on the one hand it creates the abnormal and the horrible, on the other the comic and the burlesque.
Préface p16.verification: maker compared Wikisource transcription with page image; rights and alignment need independent reader

Préface p23.text: The poetry born of Christianity, the poetry of our time, is, therefore, the drama; the real results from the wholly natural combination of two types, the sublime and the grotesque, which meet in the drama, as they meet in life and in creation.
Préface p23.verification: maker compared scan; English printed edition omits French clause le caractère du drame est le réel; do not admit as full-place equivalent without resolution

Préface p14.text: Christianity leads poetry to the truth. Like it, the modern muse will see things in a higher and broader light. It will realize that everything in creation is not humanly beautiful, that the ugly exists beside the beautiful, the unshapely beside the graceful, the grotesque on the reverse of the sublime, evil with good, darkness with light.
Préface p14.verification: maker compared Wikisource transcription with page image; rights and alignment need independent reader

Préface p14b.text: Then it is that, with its eyes fixed upon events that are both laughable and redoubtable, and under the influence of that spirit of Christian melancholy and philosophical criticism which we described a moment ago, poetry will take a great step, a decisive step, a step which, like the upheaval of an earthquake, will change the whole face of the intellectual world. It will set about doing as nature does, mingling in its creations—but without confounding them—darkness and light, the grotesque and the sublime; in other words, the body and the soul, the beast and the intellect; for the starting-point of religion is always the starting-point of poetry.
Préface p14b.verification: maker compared Wikisource transcription with page image; rights and alignment need independent reader
Préface p14b.original_scan_note: The original sentence spans French pp. 14–15; accepted packet evidence records both leaves 30 and 31. Ensure both images are read.

Préface p24.text: And so, let addle-pated pedants (one does not exclude the other) claim that the deformed, the ugly, the grotesque should never be imitated in art; one replies that the grotesque is comedy, and that comedy apparently makes a part of art. Tartuffe is not handsome, Pourceaugnac is not noble, but Pourceaugnac and Tartuffe are admirable flashes of art.
Préface p24.verification: maker compared Wikisource transcription with page image; rights and alignment need independent reader

research_update: On 19 November a separate research reader visually compared all five places with French 1912 and English 1909 scans. For Préface p23 the French clause about the character of drama as the real has no English equivalent in this printing; the translator’s exact French source edition is not established, so do not characterize the cause as proven. English p. 13 is annotated and damaged; seek a cleaner copy for exact letter review. The English title page does not name Ives; the Wikisource index attributes the translation, but independent edition-specific bibliography is still needed. Copyright 1909 is printed; actual printing date is not independently shown. This is not formal kit review.
